name: How much contingency should you budget for a commercial renovation?

mainEntity.name: How much contingency should you budget for a commercial renovation in older Los Angeles buildings?
mainEntity.text: How much contingency should you budget for a commercial renovation in older Los Angeles buildings?

acceptedAnswer.text: A contingency budget is one of the most important tools in commercial renovation planning. For many projects, setting aside 10% to 20% is a practical starting point, but older buildings, occupied spaces, and projects with incomplete drawings may require a larger reserve. Contingency is meant to cover hidden conditions, design revisions, permit-related changes, code upgrades, and unexpected coordination issues between trades. In Los Angeles-area commercial buildings, hidden electrical, plumbing, and structural issues are common enough that skipping contingency can create serious budget stress. Owners should treat contingency as part of the project budget, not as optional extra money. It is also useful to separate contingency for known unknowns from allowance items like finish selections or specialty fixtures. A disciplined budget review before demolition helps determine whether contingency should be spent, reduced, or held for real surprises. In commercial work, contingency often determines whether the project stays on track or stops halfway through unforeseen corrections.
acceptedAnswer.description: A common contingency range for commercial renovations is 10% to 20%, and older or partially unknown buildings may need more. Contingency helps cover hidden conditions, scope changes, permit corrections, and price shifts in materials or labor. The more uncertain the existing conditions, the larger the reserve should be.
